en: The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of Kālacakra. Oṃ, homage to the glorious Kālacakra!

To her who is the singular Mother consisting of the stainless emptiness of all forms, who is filled with the essence of non-dual existence, and who as a pervasive form gives birth to the lineage of the Victors—homage to her, the peace purified by innate yoga.
Having prostrated before the glorious Guru, the Lord, for the increase of the merit of people, I shall write down the sequence of the Kālacakra worship according to tradition.
First of all, that which was spoken in the glorious *Paramādibuddha*, the king of tantras, is inscribed here:
having risen from bed in the morning, one should perform the acts of cleansing and sipping water (*ācamana*).
For the sake of natural purification of the mouth, one should chew a tooth-stick or similar item;
then, having performed the water-bath, one should put on a washed garment—
a yellow garment for a householder and for the Vajrī who possesses a preceptor.
"Since it is always prescribed at the time of initiation as well as for the worship of the deity,
one should therefore perform the mantra-bath."
And thus: "First there should be bathing with water, and then there should be bathing with mantras";
therefore, one should perform the purification of the water.

And so it is said: "One should place the mantra *oṃ*, which has the nature of cleansing water, into the bathing water; with that, one should perform the bath and the worship of the deities according to the Sugata.
Herein is the bathing mantra: "Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon their birth..."
"I shall likewise bathe [the deity] with pure, divine water.
After reciting this from the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, one should then recite: *oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye hūṃ*.
With the mantra *oṃ hrīḥ svāhā*, one should perform the washing of hands and feet, sipping water (*ācamana*), and so forth;
and likewise, one should visualize the syllable *hoḥ* of yellow color upon the washed garments.
Thus,
the ritual for the satiation of the gods and others has not been written here for fear of excessive length;
thereafter, one should enter the temple of the deity.
And so it is said: "Taking a copper vessel joined with flowers and water,
one should enter the temple for the worship of the deity while remaining silent and with a tranquil mind."
In this regard, one should first perform the purification of the house;
and likewise: by means of the designation of the syllable *oṃ*, one should place the moon in a copper vessel;
with that [water], one should sprinkle water upon the ground, the seat, or the flower-offering stand.

Thus, having occupied the seat with the syllable *Haḥ* and having sat down in the vajra-posture (*vajrāsana*) or the lotus-posture (*padmāsana*), facing north, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six families (*ṣaṭkula*) and so forth.

Accordingly, it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Laghukālacakratantrarāja*: "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ haṃ kṣaḥ! O Lord of Body, Speech, Mind, and Gnosis, which consist of Wisdom and Means, make my body, speech, mind, and gnosis-vajra of the nature of vajra-amṛta; make, make the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth, devoid of intrinsic nature, svāhā!"

Having recited this mantra, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon a vajra-moon mandala, complete with its sixteen digits, transformed from the syllable *vaṃ* above the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Then, starting from that crown down to the tips of the toenails, he should cast off his own body three times like a snake shedding its skin;
thereafter, he should meditate upon himself as having the form of the moon.

For pacification and enrichment as well; therefore, in that very context, having recited "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," one should then place Oṃ, white Amitābha, on the forehead; Āḥ, red Ratnasaṃbhava, on the throat; Hūṃ, black Amoghasiddhi, at the heart; Hoḥ, yellow Vairocana, at the navel; Haṃ, dark-green Akṣobhya, on the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa); and Kṣaḥ, blue Vajrasattva, in the secret place.
And then, in that regard: "Oṃ hraḥ, O King of all weapons, destroyer of the afflictions of Māra, diamond-sharp cutter of suffering, purify my hand, svāhā.
With this mantra, one should rub hand against hand; thus it is said in the *Mūlamātṛkā* regarding the "rubbing" (*bhañjana*).

The ritual procedure for the Kālacakra worship is as follows: "The fifteen syllables from *a* to *la*—namely, *a, i, ṛ, u, lṛ; a (aṃ), e, ar, o, al; ha, ya, ra, va, la*—should be placed upon the finger-joint nodes of the left hand, beginning with the root node of the little finger. On the right hand, beginning from the upper node of the thumb and proceeding to the third node of the little finger, the letters starting with *la* should be assigned in the order of earth and the other elements: *lā, vā, rā, yā, hā; āl, au, ār, ai, ā (aḥ); lṛ, ū, ṛ, ī, ā*."

Then, having meditated on the syllable *hūṃ* of blue color within the hollow of the cupped hands between the moon and the sun, one should then form the five-pronged vajra mudrā with those seeds of the moon, sun, and Rāhu. Likewise, one should touch oneself starting from the crown of the head down to the nails of the toes;

then, one should recite this mantra: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ haṃ kṣaḥ, O Lord of body, speech, mind, and gnosis, make my vajra of body, speech, mind, and gnosis have the nature of the vajra-body, kuru kuru svāhā.*
Then, for the purification of body, speech, mind, and gnosis, one performs the ego-identification (*ahaṅkāra*): *oṃ sarvatathāgatavajrakāyasvabhāvātmako’ham*.
Then, having performed the placement of the six families (*ṣaṭkulanyāsa*), one subsequently performs the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
Having formed a hollowed cavity with both hands, one places at the heart with the pair of thumbs: *oṃ lūṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.
On the head: Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the head; at the crest-lock: Oṃ hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock;
on all limbs: Oṃ hrīṃ, huṃ to the armor.
One should touch all the limbs with both hands:
*oṃ hrāṃ netrāya vaṣaṭ* for the eyes;

*oṃ hrāḥ astrāya phaṭ* for all directions, using the snapping of the index finger and thumb—the left hand for auspicious rites and the right hand for inauspicious ones—thus one should assign the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Then, the procedure for the six-limb placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is as follows: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapon of all Tathāgatas.

Then, having mentally contemplated—through conventional usage—one's own self as the form of the glorious Kālacakra, which is the cause of the arising of the entire world like the cloudless midday sky, beyond the range [of senses], without characteristics, not an object of speech, and though unapproachable by mind, intellect, or thought, it is luminous by its very nature of existence; and having become that, one should instantly establish oneself upon the ground.
Reciting "Oṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya hūṃ," one should sprinkle pure water mixed with saffron and other substances upon the surface of the ground and construct the maṇḍala;
likewise, in the *Paramādibuddha*, it is stated: "With saffron, red sandalwood, camphor, and so forth, or even with cow dung and water..."
Having carefully observed subtle living beings, the skillful practitioner should prepare a mandala on a wooden board or a stone slab, four-cornered and measuring one cubit,
which has been washed and is smooth to the touch; there the worship of the deity should be performed.
Thus, in the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, one should construct a square maṇḍala;
and likewise: "Indeed, for the purpose of worshipping the aggregates and so forth, there is the body, speech, and mind maṇḍala."

In this context, at the time of constructing the mandala: "four-cornered" refers to the square shape; "having four gates" means it is adorned with four archways. Here, "giving" (*dāna*) consists of applying cow dung and water; "ethical discipline" (*śīla*) is the sweeping; "patience" (*kṣānti*) is the removal of hunger and thirst; and "vigorous effort" (*vīrya*) is the undertaking of the ritual action.
Meditation is the making of the mind one-pointed at that very moment, and wisdom is the brilliant, well-drawn lines; having performed the maṇḍala of the Sage, one obtains these six perfections alone.

One becomes golden-colored, free from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, and possesses a radiant splendor like the moon. Having performed these physical deeds within this excellent abode of the Sugata, one is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.

Thus, the benefits [of this] are shown by two verses. Then, with the mantra *oṃ vajralekha hūṃ*, one should place a flower in the center of the maṇḍala while touching it with that hand. Having washed the hand with *oṃ hrīḥ svāhā*, one should consecrate the lines up to their end with *oṃ sulekha sarvatathāgatā adhiṣṭhantu svāhā*.

Thereafter, one should visualize the foundational maṇḍala consisting of three layers, produced from the syllable *oṃ* and constructed from the four maṇḍalas beginning with wind, which reside within the interior of the space-maṇḍala; this should be observed according to the characteristics and the inclusion of the seats as described in the *Sādhanapadasaṃgraha*.

Then, having visualized within one's own heart an eight-petaled red lotus transformed from the syllable *paṃ*, upon its pericarp a moon disc transformed from the syllable *aṃ*, and situated therein a blue vajra transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*—which, emitting a mass of flames, fills the entire circle of the directions with a turbulent mass of fire—one should mentally invoke the Blessed One. And so it is said in the *Paramādibuddha*: "The Buddha, abiding in the *dharmadhātu*, meditated upon as indivisible from the three vajras and endowed with all sovereign qualities, should be invoked by means of the mind."
Then:
The entire threefold mandala is established as a location consisting of various colors, characterized by the aggregates, elements, and so forth, and composed of rays of gnosis.
Having meditated in the sky with the mind upon the Perfectly Awakened One, who is the essence of the mandala.

Thus [ends] the ritual procedure for the worship of Kālacakra. Then, one should visualize at the locations of the forehead, throat, heart, and navel, in sequence, the letters *aṃ*, *aḥ*, *a*, and *ā*—or alternatively, *oṃ*, *āḥ*, *hūṃ*, and *hoḥ*—as the perfected Dharma-conch, the Dharma-gong, the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), and the wish-granting tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), which are the embodiments of body, speech, mind, and gnosis. One should then emanate the Vajra-garland and other [ornaments]. As it is said: "One should emanate the many [ornaments], such as the Vajra-garland and others, from the wish-granting tree."
Vajralāsyā and the others gave an army of great wish-fulfilling jewels.
One should emanate various musical instruments for the face and so forth from the Dharma-conch;
one should emanate all musical instruments for the hands and so forth from the Dharma-vessel.
Formerly, accompanied by his fourfold army and with palms joined in reverence,
he performed a salutation to the Sage and ran swiftly before him.
When the Teacher has arrived at his own home, one should offer him an argha in the mandala.
Thus.

Having thus brought [the deities] and established the assembly of deities beginning with Kālacakra in their respective places within the support-maṇḍala, one should remove the previously offered flowers and offer a handful of flowers in the center of the maṇḍala with the mantra: *oṃ śrīkālacakrāya saparivārāyonnamaḥ*. Then, one should offer the *argha* (water for honor) with the mantra: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ śrīkālacakratraidhātukeśvara saparivāra arghaṃ praticcha tvaṃ me varado bhava*.
Having said "accept the *pādya* (water for the feet)," one should offer the *pādya*.
Thereafter, one should personally perform the washing of the feet and so forth.

And so it is said: Having purified the water in a conch shell and placed flowers and other offerings in a copper vessel, one should draw the previously described mandala and worship it with beautiful flowers.
One should indeed offer the *argha* in the mandala with the mantra of body, speech, and mind;
having performed the washing of the feet, one should again perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) in the mouth.
Thus it is said.
Then, one should go for refuge to the Three Jewels in the presence of the Blessed One.
And so it is stated: "Having placed that Victor, who is like a shadow or an illusion, upon his seat..."
Having washed his feet, he then joined his palms in reverence.
The followers of the Sugata go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

Thus, in the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, it is likewise stated: Homage to the Buddha, the Guru; homage to the Dharma, the Savior (*Tāyī*); homage to the great Saṅgha—homage perpetually to all three.
Homage to the Dharma, which possesses form and is formless, which abides on the path of merit and knowledge, and which is free from passion; and homage to the great Saṅgha.
The Jewel of the Buddha is the teacher, because from it comes the Jewel of the Dharma which is happiness;
and the Jewel of the Saṅgha is the vessel, for it can deliver one from the ocean of existence.
In the presence of the Buddhas, I reveal my own beginningless deeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world and fix my mind upon the enlightenment of the Buddhas.
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate the mind of awakening for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others.
I shall confess all misdeeds, rejoice in all merits,
and observe the fast of the noble eightfold poṣadha.
For the sake of increasing merit, I shall abstain from liquor, meat,
and sexual intercourse on the two eighth days, the two fourteenth days, on the full moon, and on the lunar day of my father.
Attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, envy, and stinginess—
all of which have their cause in striking oneself and others.
Like poison, I shall avoid all unwholesome actions and never perform them;
I shall bestow the three kinds of gifts for the sake of attaining the fruits of merit and wisdom.
I shall dwell in the four divine abodes, free from worldly attachment;
I shall make my mind pure through the four liberations and immutable.
I shall perform acts of service for the perfectly awakened Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
I shall avoid those Rākṣasas, Pretas, and Ḍākinīs who are attached to worldly desires.
I shall perform the ritual of worship for the Bodhisattvas of the Kālacakra every day;
I shall also perform the offering of food for the consumption of the wrathful gatekeepers.
I shall practice the conduct of awakening, which was practiced by the Buddhas of old—
a conduct difficult for gods and demons to perform, and one that causes great wonder.
Having fulfilled the ten perfections for the sake of enlightenment, I shall become a son of the Conqueror, and thereafter a Buddha who turns the wheel of Dharma.
Having generated the mind of awakening and being adorned with the six superknowledges, I shall invite all sentient beings to satisfy them with the nectar of Buddhahood.
Then one should begin the worship.
Thus ends the initial yoga.
Having made this aspiration, standing facing whichever direction he desires,
he should therefore begin the worship of the Perfect Buddhas, who have become the [five] aggregates.
Thus it is said.
Therefore, one should first perform the worship of the mind.
And so it is stated: "Having first performed the worship of the mind, [one should then perform] the delightful worship of the body."
Thus it is said.
Thereafter, one should perform meditation for the purpose of worship.

And so it is stated in the *Śrīvimalaprabhā*: "Then, having awakened the Tathāgatas in the expanse of the sky by means of vajra-rays within the lunar mandala, and having drawn back those rays—which were emanated for the sake of worshipping those expanded Victors—into one's own heart and visualized them as entering the moon-vajra, one should meditate upon the seed-syllables of the twelve goddesses of worship within that lunar mandala. Thereafter, one should emanate the goddesses of worship from their respective seed-syllables.
"One should worship," it is said.
And thus, the mantras therein are: "Oṃ c ch j jh ña vajragandhe gandhārcanaṃ kuru svāhā."
Oṃ c ch j jh ñā vajramāle, perform the offering of garlands, svāhā!
Oṃ ṭ ṭh ḍ ḍh ṇa vajradhūpe, perform the offering of incense, svāhā!
Oṃ ṭ ṭh ḍ ḍh ṇā vajradīpe, perform the offering of lamps, svāhā!

In the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*: Oṃ p ph b bh ma vajrāmṛte vajra naivedya-pūjāṃ kuru svāhā.
Oṃ p ph b bh mā vajrāmṛte, perform the worship with unbroken grains and fruit, svāhā!
Oṃ t th d dh na vajralāsye, perform the worship with vajra ornaments, svāhā!
Oṃ t th d dh nā vajrahāsye, perform the worship with the bell and mirror, svāhā!
Oṃ k kh g gh ṅa vajravādye vādyapūjāṃ kuru svāhā | Oṃ k kh g gh ṅā vajranṛtye nṛtyapūjāṃ kuru svāhā | Oṃ s ṣ ś ka vajragīte gītapūjāṃ kuru svāhā |

*Oṃ sa~ pa~ ṣa~ śa~ kā~ vajrakāme, perform for all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Krodhas, and others, a vajra-natured offering of supreme bliss, svāhā!* With these mantra-words of the Goddess, this is the "mind-made" (*manomaya*) offering. Thereafter, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) makes a great petition to the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) and so forth.
Today, for me who delights in the worship of the Buddha, the great wish-fulfilling tree has flourished.
Give me divine flowers of supreme color and fragrance;
give me now gośīrṣaka and other perfumes, incense, and so forth.
Powders, food offerings, and various garments, as well as diverse fruits,
stainless parasols, and canopies of great majesty.
O supreme great wish-fulfilling jewel, for me who delights in the worship of the Buddha,
grant, grant a garland of lamps that destroys the darkness!
Jeweled ornaments and the seven precious gems,
the Dharma-conch of great sound, and whatever mouth-instruments there may be;
Give me all those [instruments] for the worship of the Buddha today:
the great-sounding Dharma-gaṇḍī and whatever hand-held musical instruments there are.
