The term "devī" does not appear in the Mūlamātṛkā.
O Kālacakra, grant all these things today to me, who am devoted to the worship of the Buddhas;
having fashioned them, bestow flowers upon Śākyasiṃha on this earth.
O Sage, just as these were offered by Śakra, so do I offer my own riches to you, who are like a god among men, a lord of asuras, and a king of serpents.
Thus have they been given, and I shall likewise give them with a mind free from dark deeds.
Thus:
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Puṣpaketurāja.
It is as follows: Oṃ puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpodbhave puṣpasaṃbhave puṣpāvakīrṇe svāhā.
Having recited this three times, one should consecrate the flowers.
Furthermore, having consecrated the entire collection of substances with the syllable *ha* or *hoḥ*, one should touch them with the *vajra-mudrā*.
Thus, the flowers, perfumes, and so forth, once touched, become purified and protected.
Then one should purify and awaken the food offering (naivedya) for the first consumer of the oblation (balibhoktṛ).
Thus it is said.

Then, one should perform worship with the mantra accompanied by the seed-syllable (bīja). And so it is stated: "This worship with the seed-syllable is proclaimed for the purpose of honoring the True Dharma."
Thus it is said.
And that mantra must be concluded with "Namaḥ" (homage).
Accordingly, it is stated in the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*: "O Lord of Men, in rites of nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the mantra ends in 'Svāhā'; in rites of pacification (*śāntika*), it ends in 'Namaḥ'."
And so forth.
Therein, in the center of the mandala: Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Śrī Kālacakra.
Oṃ haiṃ, homage to Viśvamātṛ.
Oṃ a, homage to Akṣobhya. Oṃ aṃ, homage to Vajrasattva.
Oṃ āḥ, homage to Vajradhātvīśvarī.
"Oṃ āḥ, homage to Prajñāpāramitā!
With these mantra-syllables, one should offer flowers using the thumb and ring finger.

Then, with respect to the worshippers, since the eastern direction is that which faces the Blessed One situated in the center of the maṇḍala, whereas the direction facing the worshippers is behind the Blessed One, one should perform the worship starting from the front.
And so it is stated in the Paramādibuddha: "Whichever of the four cardinal directions he may face, that [direction] is the front for him; the mandala is drawn there."
Thus it is said.

In the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, regarding the arrangement of the world-system and the passions of sentient beings, there is a fixed determination of the directions such as the east according to the rising and setting of the sun on each continent.

And so it is stated in the *Laghu-kālacakra-tantrarāja*: "O King, for all people, the king of mountains stands to the north; the rising of the sun occurs in the east, and it sets in the west at the time of the mountain."

Then, having uttered the unstruck (*anāhata*) syllables beginning with *A*, which are characterized by being unobstructed, one should perform the meditation on the Blessed One—who stands in the center of the maṇḍala-cakra drawn according to the fixed arrangement of the continents and peaks (such as the black peak of Pūrvavideha) situated before Mount Sumeru within the entire world-system that has arisen from the five symbols—possessing the specific characteristics of the Mind-Cakra and so forth, such as the black color in the east and so on. However, in the case of the pledge-offering (*samayapūjā*), because the deity Citta-vajra alone is predominant based on all the ritual actions of the worshipper’s inclinations and so forth, one should worship the deities Kṛṣṇadīpta and the others in the directions starting from the east.
Oṃ āḥ, homage to Kṛṣṇadīptā in the east. Oṃ āḥ, homage to Raktadīptā.
In the south:
Oṃ aḥ, homage to Śvetadīptā. In the west:
Oṃ āḥ, homage to Pītadīptā in the north;
thus, according to the sequence of emanation, in the cardinal directions.
Oṃ hoḥ, homage to Pradīpā; in the northwest. Oṃ haṃ, homage to Khadyotā.
In the northeast: Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to Marīcikā. In the southwest:
Oṃ haḥ, homage to Dhūmā; in the southeast.
Thus, in the intermediate directions, according to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).
Then, in the four corners behind the goddesses:
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Cintāmaṇi.
In the southeast (Agni):
Oṃ āḥ, homage to Dharmagaṇḍī; in the southwest.
Oṃ oṃ, homage to Dharmaśaṅkha.
In the northeast: Oṃ hoḥ, salutation to the Kalpavṛkṣa (Wish-fulfilling Tree).
In the northwest:
Then, again, in the place of the Blessed One himself, according to the distinctions of mind, speech, body, and gnosis: *oṃ buddhāya namaḥ* | *oṃ dharmāya namaḥ* |
Oṃ, homage to the Saṃgha. Oṃ, homage to the Svabhāvakāya.
Oṃ, homage to the Dharmakāya.
Oṃ, homage to the Saṃbhogakāya!
Oṃ, homage to the Nirmāṇakāya!
Oṃ, homage to Jñānavajra!
Oṃ, homage to the Mind-Vajra.
Oṃ, homage to the Speech-Vajra. Oṃ, homage to the Body-Vajra.
Oṃ, homage to the four liberations.
Oṃ, homage to the four divine abodes.
Oṃ, homage to the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.
Oṃ, homage to the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma!
Oṃ, homage to those who teach all Dharmas!
Oṃ, homage to the Three Jewels!
Oṃ, homage to Śākyamuni!
Then, in the four corners at the locations of the goddesses,
[one offers] "Oṃ, homage to Dānapāramitā."
Oṃ, homage to the perfection of ethical discipline. Oṃ, homage to the perfection of patience. Oṃ, homage to the perfection of vigor.
Then, in the place of the previously mentioned Kṛṣṇadīptā:
Oṃ, homage to Dhyānapāramitā.
Then, in the place of Viśvamātṛ.
Oṃ, homage to Prajñāpāramitā!
Then, in the places such as the red, blazing [directions] and so forth:
Oṃ, homage to Upāyapāramitā!
Oṃ! Aspiration. 1. What is this "Kālacakra Ritual of Worship"? Homage to the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā)!
Oṃ! Homage to the Perfection of Power (Balapāramitā)!
Then, again, in the center:
Oṃ, homage to the Perfection of Wisdom.
Oṃ, homage to all symbols. Oṃ, homage to all oceans.
Then, according to the order of emanation, in the cardinal directions starting from the east where the Goddess is located externally:
Oṃ i, homage to Amoghasiddhi;
Oṃ ṛ, homage to Ratnasambhava.
Oṃ u, homage to Amitābha.
Oṃ lṛ, homage to Vairocana. Then, in the intermediate directions beginning with the northwest, in the order of withdrawal: Oṃ lṛ, homage to Locanā.
Oṃ, homage to Māmakī.
Oṃ Ṛ, homage to Pāṇḍarā. Oṃ Ī, homage to Tārā.
Then, in the eastern direction connected to the upper [level], at the location of the door of the *cittacakra*:
Oṃ Haṃ, homage to the victory-pot of *bodhicitta*.
Then, to Amoghasiddhi and the others, in the southern directions.
In the east and the other directions: Oṃ hi, obeisance to the jar of urine;
Oṃ hr, obeisance to the jar of blood;
Oṃ hu, obeisance to the jar of marrow.
Oṃ laṃ, homage to Viḍghaṭa. Then, to the left [of] Vairocana and the others, starting from the west: Oṃ hlṛ, homage to Viḍghaṭa;
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Majjāghaṭa.
Oṃ, homage to the red jar. Oṃ hī, homage to the urine jar.
Then, below that connection, in the western direction, as before.
Oṃ haḥ, homage to the victory-pitcher composed of passion (rajas).
Alternatively: Oṃ haṃ hi hṛ hu hlṛ, homage to the victory-pitchers. Oṃ hlṛ hū hū hī haḥ, homage to the victory-pitchers.
Thus, one should offer flowers in these places in sequence, or two handfuls of flowers. Then, on the left side of the southern gate: Oṃ a vajrapāṇaye namaḥ.
Then, on the right sides of the eastern and other doors:
Oṃ E, homage to Khagarbha;
Oṃ Ar, homage to Kṣitigarbha.
Oṃ oṃ, homage to Lokeśvara. Oṃ al, homage to Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
Then, at the left of the eastern gate.
Oṃ aṃ, homage to Samantabhadra. Then, on the left of the northern gate: Oṃ aḥ, homage to Śabdavajrā.
Then, in the corners beginning with the northwest: Oṃ āl, homage to Gandhavajrā.
Oṃ auḥ, homage to Rūpavajrā. Oṃ āḥ, homage to Rasavajrā. Oṃ aiḥ, homage to Sparśavajrā.
Then, on the left of the western gate: Oṃ ā dharmadhātuvajrāya namaḥ. Then, in the middle of the gates starting from the east: Oṃ ya vighnāntakāya namaḥ.
In its lap: Oṃ lāḥ stambhinyai namaḥ.
Thus: Oṃ ra, homage to Prajñāntaka;
Oṃ vāḥ, homage to Māninī;
Oṃ va, homage to Prajñāntaka.
Oṃ rāḥ, homage to Jambhinī!
Oṃ la, homage to Yamāntakā!
Oṃ yāḥ, homage to Ativīryā!
Then, on the eastern archway connected to the upper [level], *oṃ k kh g gh ṅa vajravādyāyai namaḥ*. Then, on the left altars outside the gates starting from the east:
*oṃ c ch j jh ña vajragandhāyai namaḥ*.
Oṃ ṭ ṭh ḍ ḍh ṇa vajradhūpāyai namaḥ | Oṃ p ph b bh ma vajrāmṛtāyai namaḥ | Oṃ t th d dh na vajralāsyāyai namaḥ |
Then, at the western archway connected to the netherworld (*pātāla*):
*oṃ s ṣ ś h kṣa vajragītāyai namaḥ*. At the southern archway:
Oṃ s ṣ ś h kṣā, homage to Vajrākāmā.
Then, on the altars to the right, beginning from the west:
Oṃ t th d dh nā, homage to Vajrahāsyā.
Oṃ p ph b bh mā, homage to Vajrarājākṣatā!
Oṃ ṭ ṭh ḍ ḍh ṇā, homage to Vajradīpā!
Oṃ c ch j jh ña, homage to Vajramālā!
Then, at the northern archway:
Oṃ k kh g gh ṅā vajranṛtyāyai namaḥ.
Alternatively, [place] first—

In the *Kālacakratantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, having placed the syllable *Oṃ* and recited the previously mentioned short seed-syllables, one should offer a handful of flowers with the words "Homage to the six offering goddesses" (*namaḥ ṣaṭ-pūjā-devībhyah*). Likewise, this is done with the long seed-syllables as well; such is the worship of the mind-maṇḍala.
Then, in the speech-maṇḍala, one should first offer *oṃ ha vajracarcikāyai namaḥ* in the east;
thereafter, having established the first petal facing this [deity], one should worship the goddesses of the eight petals by proceeding clockwise around the eight-petaled lotus.
Therein: Oṃ hi, obeisance to Bhīmā; Oṃ ya, obeisance to Ugrā;
Oṃ yi, obeisance to Kāladaṃṣṭrā.
Oṃ yṛ, homage to Jvaladanalamukhā; Oṃ hī, homage to Vāyuvegā;
Oṃ yu, homage to Pracaṇḍā.
Oṃ ylṛ, obeisance to Rudrākṣī; Oṃ yaṃ, obeisance to Sthūlanāsā;
then to the south.
Oṃ haḥ, homage to Vajravārāhī; here too, it is the same as before:
Oṃ hṛ, homage to Kaṅkālī.
Oṃ ra, homage to Kālarātri; Oṃ ri, homage to Prakupitavadanā;
Oṃ ha, homage to Kāladaṃṣṭrā.
Oṃ hrāṃ, homage to Karālī; Oṃ rāṃ, homage to Kālī; Oṃ lṝ, homage to Ghorā.
Oṃ raṃ, homage to Virūpā;
then to the left,
Oṃ haṃ, homage to Vajrarātrī Raudrī.
As before:
Oṃ hu, obeisance to Gaurī; Oṃ va, obeisance to Gaṅgā.
Oṃ, obeisance to Vinṛtyā; Oṃ, obeisance to Vṛparamatvaritā;
Oṃ Hūṃ, obeisance to Totalā.
Oṃ vu, homage to Lakṣaṇā; Oṃ vlṛ, homage to Piṅgalā;
Oṃ vaṃ, homage to Kṛṣṇā.
Then, in the west: Oṃ hā, homage to Vajrendrāṇī,
as before.
Oṃ hlṛ, homage to Vajrābhā! Oṃ la, homage to Vajragātrā!
Oṃ li, homage to Varakanakavatī!
Oṃ la, homage to Urvaśī; Oṃ halṛ, homage to Citralekhā;
Oṃ lu, homage to Rambhā.
Oṃ llṛ, obeisance to Ahalyā; Oṃ laṃ, obeisance to Sutārā;
then in the northwestern direction.
Oṃ kṣā, homage to Vajrabrāhmaṇī,
as before;
Oṃ kṣlṛ, homage to Sāvitrī.
Oṃ lā, homage to Padmanetrā; Oṃ lī, homage to Jalajavatī;
Oṃ lṛ, homage to Buddhi.
Oṃ kṣlṛ, homage to Vāgīśvarī;
Oṃ lū, homage to Gāyatrī;
Oṃ llū, homage to Vidyutī.
Oṃ laḥ, salutation to Smṛti;
then in the Īśāna direction, Oṃ kṣaṃ, salutation to Vajralakṣmī.
And likewise: Oṃ kṣu, obeisance to Śvetā; Oṃ vā, obeisance to Candralekhā;
Oṃ vī, obeisance to Śaśadharavadanā.
Oṃ vṛ, obeisance to Vṛhaṃsavarṇā;
Oṃ kṣū, obeisance to Dhṛti; Oṃ vū, obeisance to Padmeśā.
Oṃ vlṛ, homage to Tāranetrā;
Oṃ vaḥ, homage to Vimalaśaśadharā;
then in the southwest.
Oṃ kṣaḥ, homage to Vajrakaumārī;
likewise, Oṃ kṣa, homage to Padmā;
Oṃ rā, homage to Anaṅgā.
Oṃ rī, homage to Kumārī; oṃ, homage to Mṛgapatigamanā;
oṃ kṣa, homage to Ratnamālā, h kṣa.
Oṃ rū, obeisance to Sunetrā; Oṃ ralṛ, obeisance to Klīnā;
Oṃ ra, obeisance to Bhadrā.
Then, in the fire: Oṃ kṣa, obeisance to Vajravaiṣṇavī;
likewise, Oṃ kṣi, obeisance to Śrī.
Oṃ yā, obeisance to Māyā; Oṃ yī, obeisance to Kīrti; Oṃ yṛ, obeisance to Lakṣmī.
Oṃ kṣī, homage to the most supreme Vijayā; Oṃ yū, homage to Śrī Jayā, the tongue; Oṃ ylṛ, homage to Śrī Jayantī. [This is] the ritual procedure for the worship of the Kālacakra. Oṃ vi pra. Homage.
Oṃ ylṛ, homage to Śrī Jayantī.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Śrīcakra;
or else, having worshipped the principal goddess, [one recites]:
Oṃ hi yayi yṛ hī yu ylṛ yaṃ, obeisance to the goddesses of the eight petals beginning with Bhīmā.
With this, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*); in this manner, one should proceed everywhere. Then, on the left altar (*vedikā*) of the southern gate, in sequential order:
Oṃ kaḥ, homage to the desire for killing;
oṃ khaḥ, homage to the desire for sexual union; oṃ gaḥ, homage to the desire for scratching.
Oṃ Ghaḥ, obeisance to the desire for torment and shade; Oṃ Ṅaḥ, obeisance to the desire for crushing all limbs—
likewise on the left side of the eastern gate.
Oṃ caḥ, homage to Vidveṣecchā; Oṃ chaḥ, homage to Aṃśukecchā;
Oṃ jaḥ, homage to Uccāṭanecchā.
Oṃ jhaḥ, homage to the desire for touch;
Oṃ ñaḥ, homage to the desire to consume what has been cast off—
likewise on the left side of the southern gate.
Oṃ ṭaḥ, homage to the desire for paralysis; Oṃ ṭhaḥ, homage to the desire for beauty; Oṃ ḍaḥ, homage to the desire for food.
Oṃ ḍhaḥ, obeisance to Ākṛṣṭīcchā; Oṃ ṇaḥ, obeisance to Saṃgrāmecchā;
then, on the left side of the left door.
Oṃ paḥ, homage to the desire for prosperity; Oṃ phaḥ, homage to the desire for ornaments;
Oṃ baḥ, homage to the desire for gentle speech.
Oṃ bhaḥ, homage to the desire for binding; oṃ maḥ, homage to the desire for reviling children;
then, on the left of the western gate.
Oṃ taḥ, homage to the desire for paralyzing; Oṃ thaḥ, homage to the desire for pinning;
Oṃ daḥ, homage to the desire for binding with serpents.
Oṃ dhaḥ, homage to Gandhecchā;
Oṃ naḥ, homage to Bandhanecchā. Then, [proceed] to the eastern gate itself.
Oṃ saḥ, obeisance to the desire for eradication; Oṃ paḥ, obeisance to the desire for playing musical instruments;
Oṃ ṣaḥ, obeisance to the desire for running.
Oṃ śaḥ, homage to the desire to deceive sentient beings;
Oṃ kaḥ, homage to the desire to expel phlegm;
then, on the left of the left door.
Oṃ laḥ, obeisance to the one who desires much quarreling; Oṃ vaḥ, obeisance to the one who desires bodily impurity;
Oṃ raḥ, obeisance to the one who desires a seat; Oṃ yaḥ, obeisance to the one who desires immersion.
Oṃ haḥ, homage to the desire for lying down; then, on the left of the western door,
oṃ kṣaḥ, homage to the desire for the discharge of feces and urine.
Oṃ kṣaḥ, salutation to Nṛtyecchā;
Oṃ kṣaḥ, salutation to Rājyecchā.
Alternatively, having placed the syllable Oṃ at the beginning and uttered all the seed-syllables, [one says]: "Salutation to the thirty-six Goddesses of Desire."
Thus one should offer a handful of flowers; this is the worship of the Vāk-maṇḍala. Then, in the eastern gate of the Kāya-maṇḍala, on the left:
Oṃ Kaḥ, homage to Vajravaiṣṇavī; in the place of her lap: Oṃ Gṛ, homage to Śrī.

Likewise, on this very seat consisting of four, eight, or sixteen [petals], one should worship the goddesses of the petals by starting from the petal facing this [central deity] and proceeding clockwise among the petals of the three-layered lotus;
there, in the first four petals: Oṃ Ṅaṅa Vajrāyai Namaḥ.
Oṃ ṅiṅi vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ ṅū ṅū vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ ṅu ṅu vajrāyai dārakakrīḍanecchā ni yo, pṛ kālacakratantralaghugranthasaṃgrahe namaḥ ||
[Then, on the eight petals: Oṃ ḍlṛ ḍlṛ vajrāyai namaḥ;
oṃ ṅaṃ ṅaṃ vajrāyai namaḥ;
oṃ gha gha vajrāyai namaḥ.
Oṃ ghi ghi vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ ghṛ ghṛ vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ ghughu vajrāyai namaḥ |
Oṃ ghlṛ ghlṛ, homage to Vajrā;
Oṃ ghaṃ ghaṃ, homage to Vajrā.
Then, upon the sixteen petals:
Oṃ ga ga vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ gigi vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ gṛ gṛ vajrāyai namaḥ |
Oṃ gu gu vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ glṛ glṛ vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ gaṃ gaṃ vajrāyai namaḥ |
Oṃ kha kha vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ khi khi vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ khū khṛ vajrāyai namaḥ ||
Oṃ khu khu, homage to Vajrā;
oṃ khlṛ khlṛ, homage to Vajrā;
oṃ khaṃ khaṃ, homage to Vajrā.
Oṃ ka ka vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ ki ki vajrāyai namaḥ | Oṃ kṛ kṛ vajrāyai namaḥ ||
Oṃ oṃ ku ku vajrāyai namaḥ,
oṃ klṛ klṛ vajrāyai namaḥ— thus [are the mantras] for the goddesses on the petals, on the exterior.
Then, to the south of this very door,
[one should worship] with "Oṃ Caṃ, obeisance to Vajra-Nairṛti.
Here too, in the same manner, one should worship the goddesses of the petals using the letters beginning with *ña* from the *ca*-group, according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).
Then, to the left of the southern gate:
Oṃ ṭaṃ namo vajravahnaye;
likewise, with the letters beginning with ṇa from the ṭa-group.
Then, to the right of the left door:
Oṃ Paṃ Vajrasamudrāya Namaḥ; likewise here, with the *pavarga* [consonants].
Then, at the left side of the western gate:
"Oṃ Taṃ, obeisance to Vajrendra"; likewise here, with the *tavarga* (the dental consonant group).
Then, to the left of the left door: Oṃ saṃ vajrarudrāya namaḥ;
in his lap: Oṃ sṛ vajrapārvatyai namaḥ.
Then, in the same manner here, with the same group of vowels, [one should worship] at the left of the next door: *oṃ kṣaḥ vajradhanadāyai namaḥ*.
On her lap: Oṃ ṣlṛ, obeisance to Vajradhaneśā.
Then, here, one should worship all [the goddesses] in the order of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama) with long vowels;
the sequence there is as follows, first on the four petals:
Oṃ sā sā, homage to Vajrā; oṃ sī sī, homage to Vajrā;
oṃ sṝ sṛ, homage to Vajrā.
Oṃ sū sū, homage to Vajrā;
then, on the eight petals: Oṃ slṛ slṛ, homage to Vajrā.
Oṃ saḥ saḥ, homage to Vajrā; Oṃ pā pā, homage to Vajrā;
Oṃ pī pī, homage to Vajrā.
Oṃ, homage to Pṛvajrā; Oṃ × pū × pū, homage to Pūvajrā;
Oṃ × plṛ × plṛ, homage to Plṛvajrā.
Oṃ — paḥ × paḥ, homage to Vajrā;
likewise, on the sixteen petals:
Oṃ ṣā ṣā, homage to Vajrā.
Oṃ ṣī ṣī, homage to Vajrā;
Oṃ ṣṛ ṣṣṛ, homage to Vajrā;
Oṃ ṣū ṣū, homage to Vajrā.
Oṃ ṣlṛ ṣlṛ, homage to Vajrā;
Oṃ ṣaḥ ṣaḥ, homage to Vajrā;
Oṃ śā śā, homage to Vajrā.
Oṃ śī śī, homage to Vajrā; oṃ śṛ śṛ, homage to Vajrā;
oṃ śū śū, homage to Vajrā.
Oṃ ślṛ ślṛ, homage to Vajrā; oṃ śaḥ śaḥ, homage to Vajrā;
oṃ kṣā kṣā, homage to Vajrā.
Oṃ kṣī kṣī, homage to Vajrā;
oṃ kṣa kṣa, homage to Vajrā;
oṃ kṣū kṣū, homage to Vajrā.
Oṃ kṣlṛ kṣlṛ, homage to Vajrā. This is the ritual procedure for the worship of Kālacakra from the *Kālacakratantra-laghugranthasaṃgraha*. Then, in the northwest: Oṃ naḥ, homage to Vajrabrahmā.
Likewise, here, with the long *tā* from the *tavarga* (the dental class) beginning with *ta*, then in the northeast: *oṃ maḥ vajragaṇendrāya namaḥ*.
Likewise, here with the labial class (pavarga), then in the southwest: Oṃ ṇaḥ, obeisance to Vajrakārtikeya.
Likewise, here with the *ṭa*-group,
then in the southeast: Oṃ Ñaḥ, obeisance to Vajravāyu.
Likewise, here with the *ca*-group, then on the left of the southern gate: Oṃ Ṅaḥ Vajrayamāya Namaḥ.
On her lap: *oṃ glṛ vajrayāminyai namaḥ*.
Then, in the same manner here, with the *ka*-group beginning with *kā* in its long form, or else in each of the twelve individual lotuses.
Having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, the seed-syllables as previously stated in the middle,
and at the end: "Oṃ, homage to the twenty-eight Vajras and lunar days (*tithi*)!"
Thus one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
Then, in the upper [direction] and the east:
*Oṃ haṃ, homage to Uṣṇīṣacakravartin*.
On her lap: Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to Atinīlā.
Then, in the middle of the eastern gate: Oṃ yaṃ, obeisance to Nīladaṇḍā;
Oṃ lā, obeisance to Mārīcī.
Then, to the south:
Oṃ raṃ, homage to Ṭakkirāja;
Oṃ vā, homage to Cundā.
In the north: Oṃ vaṃ, homage to Acalā;
Oṃ rā, homage to Bhṛkuṭī.
In the west: Oṃ laṃ, homage to Mahābalā.
Oṃ yā, homage to Vajraśṛṅkhalā.
Below that, in the west:
Oṃ ha, obeisance to Suṃbharājñī;
Oṃ hā, obeisance to Raudrākṣī.
Then, at the eastern archway above:
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Jayā. Then, at the bases of the left pillars of the archways of the doors starting from the east:
Oṃ hya, homage to Padma. Oṃ hra, homage to Vāsuki.
Oṃ hra, homage to Kulika.
Oṃ hva, homage to Takṣaka.
Then, in the western archway of the netherworld (pātāla):
Oṃ kṣla (kṣa), homage to Vijayā.
Then, at the bases of the archway pillars starting from the western door:
Oṃ hrāḥ, obeisance to Mahāpadma;
Oṃ hvāḥ, obeisance to Ananta.
Oṃ hrāḥ, homage to Śaṅkhapāla!
Oṃ hyāḥ, homage to Karkoṭaka!

Then, one should worship the goddess Icchā on the altar of the maṇḍala of speech using those same seed-syllables, but here one should worship the goddess Pratīcchā with [those syllables] accompanied by the anusvāra.
There, in order, on the left altar-platform (vedikā) of the southern gate, in the rows [of seats]:
Oṃ kaṃ, obeisance to Māraṇapratīcchā; Oṃ khaṃ, obeisance to Maithunapratīcchā.
Oṃ gaṃ, homage to her who accepts scratching. Oṃ ghaṃ, homage to her who accepts the removal of heat. Oṃ ṅaṃ, homage to her who accepts the massaging of all limbs.
Likewise, on the left side of the eastern gate, there is the desire for [acts such as] inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*) and so forth, by means of the five *ca*-group seed-syllables.
In the same manner, this occurs on the left side of the southern gate and in the northern, western, and other directions according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).
Again, it is likewise on the left altars (*vedikā*) of the eastern and other directions, excluding the southern one.

Alternatively, having placed the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning and all the seed-syllables (*bījas*) in the middle, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the mantra: "Salutation to the thirty-six Goddesses of Reception (*pratīcchā-devīs*) at the end.

Then, in the locations starting from the east, [one worships] Kālacakra, Kuvera, Īśāna, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Vināyaka, Kārttikeya, Nandin, Mahākāla, the planetary guardians (*graha-pālas*), the lunar mansion guardians (*nakṣatra-pālas*), the Lord of the Gods (*surendra*), the Lord of the Asuras (*asurendra*), and the Lord of Serpents (*phaṇīndra*). Thus is the ritual procedure for the worship of Kālacakra.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the Wheel of Dharma! Oṃ āḥ, homage to the Auspicious Vase!
Oṃ oṃ, homage to the Drum!
Oṃ hoḥ, homage to the Kalpavṛkṣa tree. Then, in the east above: Oṃ hā, homage to Vajrākṣī.
Then, outside of that, in the cremation grounds starting from the east: Oṃ ka kha ga gha ṅa vajraśvānāsyāyai namaḥ | Oṃ kṣa ya ra va la vajraśūkarāsyāyai namaḥ |
Oṃ ha ya ra va la, homage to Vajravyāghrāsyā.
Oṃ sa pa ṣa śa kṣa (ka), homage to Vajrajambūkāsyā.
Then, in the west, is Pātālasaṃ.
Oṃ haṃ, homage to Nīlā. Then, in the cremation grounds beginning from the northwest (vāyavya): Oṃ ta tha da dha na, homage to Garuḍāsyā.
Oṃ pa pha ba bha ma, homage to Ulūkāsyā.
Oṃ ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa, homage to Gṛdhrāsyā. Oṃ ca cha ja jha ña, homage to Kākāsyā.
Then, right here in the circle of the cemetery foundation, in the northeast:
Oṃ Aṃ, homage to Vajracandra. In the southwest:
Oṃ āḥ, homage to Vajrasūrya.
Then, Oṃ, homage to the various vajra-born ones, to the hosts of deities numbering three and a half crores located in the pores of the body and hair-follicles.
One should worship the external deities.
Oṃ, homage to Vajrabudha.
Oṃ, homage to Vajramaṅgala.
Oṃ, homage to Vajraśukra.
Oṃ, homage to Vajrabṛhaspati.
Oṃ, homage to Vajraśanaiścara.
Oṃ, homage to Vajraketu.
Oṃ, homage to Vajra Rāhu.
Oṃ, homage to Vajra Kālāgni.
Oṃ, homage to Vajra Dhruva.
Oṃ, homage to Vajrāgastya. Oṃ, homage to the Vajra constellations. Oṃ, homage to the twelve Vajra zodiac signs.
Oṃ, homage to the sixteen Vajra digits.
Oṃ, homage to Nandikeśvara. Oṃ, homage to Vajramahākāla.
Oṃ, homage to Vajraghaṇṭākarṇa!
Oṃ, homage to Vajrabhṛṅgin!
Oṃ, homage to the Vajra-kṣetrapālas!
Oṃ, homage to all the Vajra-messengers!
Oṃ, homage to Hārītī!
Oṃ, homage to all accomplishments!
Oṃ, homage to the Guru, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas!
Then, one should worship the Blessed One with the sixteen-line mantra.
Therein, this is the mantra: Homage to Vajrasattva!
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
Homage to the kings of the Vajra Wrathful Deities!
Homage to Viśvamātā!
Homage to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Goddesses!
Homage to the Vajra-Ḍākinīs!

Homage to the Blessed One Kālacakra, who is terrifying like Vajrabhairava; whose body is the color of a great sapphire (māhendranīla); whose white and red feet trample upon the hearts of Māras and afflictions; whose necks are black, red, and white; whose faces are fierce, formidable, and terrifying with fangs that are blue, white, yellow, and red; whose right and left shoulders are black, red, and white; who has twelve arms and twenty-six hands; whose hands hold a vajra, sword, trident, knife, arrow, goad, *ḍamaru* drum, mallet, discus, spear, staff, axe, vajra-bell, shield, *khaṭvāṅga*, skull-cup, bow, noose, jewel, lotus, conch, mirror, chain, the head of Brahmā, and an elephant hide; who is clothed in a tiger skin; who has a garland of severed heads hanging from his shoulder; who wears a vajra-band crown on his head and bears a vajra-skull garland and a crescent moon; who is adorned with earrings, bracelets, a necklace, a belt, anklets, ashes, a sacred thread, a crest-jewel, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), and the lord of serpents; whose heart is pleased by the Vajra-Ḍākinīs; and whose feet are praised by Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Bhūtendra, and Narendra.

I bow to that which has no end, beginning, or middle; no state of existence, death, or birth; no sound, smell, taste, touch, or form; no mind, nor primordial nature (prakṛti) or spirit (puruṣa); no bondage or liberation, and no agent; no seed, manifest world, or time; and which, throughout all the worlds, is neither the nature of suffering nor happiness—a Nirvāṇa that is signless, devoid of instruments of perception, and free from qualities.

I pay homage to Kālacakra—the Vajra of Time, the peerless Puruṣa, all-pervading, free from conceptual proliferation, immutable; whose ears, nose, mouth, eyes, and head are everywhere, and whose hands and feet are on all sides; the end of beings and the lord of beings, the bearer of the boon of the three worlds, the cause of causes, the primordial knowledge, attainable through yoga, the state of supreme bliss.

I bow to that Visarga, the creator in the form of power, resembling lightning and fire, possessing the brilliance of twelve suns, knowledge with the luster of a thunderbolt, and the means for reaching the supreme state.
I bow to that Bindu in the form of nectar, white, the lord of the three worlds, which flows from the moon, abides at the crown of the world, destroys death, and crushes the fear of worldly existence.

I bow to Vajrasattva, the Lord of the World, who is pure consciousness in the form of mantra, surrounded by the thirty gods; whose nature is both suffering and bliss, appearing peaceful to the virtuous and experiencing the fruit of their good deeds, yet appearing terrible to the wicked; he who, according to the law, produces in the mind whatever fruit corresponds to the karma one has performed—he who is the universal form and the progenitor of the three worlds.

One who is neither one nor even many, equal yet equalizing the unequal, present on the right, left, front, back, above, below, and indeed all around; whose single form possesses the colors white, green, and the great variegated spectrum; who is short, long, and protracted, yet devoid of qualities and yet possessed of qualities; who is female, male, and neither male nor female; the sole support of all, the auspicious and supreme fortune—to You, homage! To You, homage! To You, homage!

In the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, homage to the glorious Kālacakra, whose nature is emptiness and compassion, the single embodiment of the knowledge and the object of knowledge regarding the non-existence of the arising and destruction of the three realms of existence.

Having offered a handful of flowers with these or other verses of salutation, one should perform a prostration preceded by the eight-limbed gesture (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇati*) and utter the praise. Then: *oṃ vajrapuṣpe āḥ hūṃ svāhā*.
Oṃ vajradhūpe āḥ hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajradīpe āḥ hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajragandhe āḥ hūṃ svāhā |
Oṃ vajramālye āḥ hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajranaivedye āḥ hūṃ svāhā | With such mantra phrases, one should perform worship according to one's capacity with special materials such as gold and silver.
Then, one should again perform the confession of sins and so forth:

"May the Blessed One, Śrī Kālacakra—the one who has directly perceived the wheel of phenomena (bhāvacakra) encompassing all times, together with the wheel of deities within the maṇḍala—attend to me! Whatever unwholesome [action] I have committed, caused to be committed, or rejoiced in, whether knowingly or unknowingly, in this life or in other lives, I confess it all before you."

"From this moment forth, I shall never again [commit such acts], especially [those directed against] the Sons of the Sugatas, the Sugatas themselves, the followers of the Sugatas, the disciples of the Sugatas, and the Pratyekajinas; I rejoice in all the merit performed by those who have not yet become progenitors [of the Dharma]. I entreat all the Buddhas—who possess the eightfold limbs of the Tāstavya, who have cast off all partiality and distraction, and who have set in motion the Wheel of Dharma that was previously unturned—to turn the Wheel of Dharma. I entreat all the Victors who have attained Parinirvāṇa, who are the ultimate refuge for the helpless, and who have completed what was to be done, so that they may dwell forever without agitation, removing the fear of the torments of discipline for those who are deluded and deprived. May the world attain the incomparable Great Bliss arising from the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion, unstained by the blemish of false conceptualization. Thus I dedicate the merit.
I offer myself for all services and attendance to the entire assembly of the sons of the Conquerors, beginning with Puṣya, who are overwhelmed by supreme compassion.
For the sake of the perfect awakening of all sentient beings, I generate the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).

I shall bear the vajra, the bell, the mudrā, and the Guru upon my head; I shall give gifts to the desired Vajra; I shall maintain the commitment (samaya) of the Supreme Victor toward the Jewel; and here, in the Wheel, I shall uphold it.

I perform worship in the family of the manifest lotus; I maintain the vow in the family that gives birth to the Victors for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings; and I generate the mind of enlightenment.
The sons of the Conquerors have done, will do, and are doing [this];
from this moment forth, I shall likewise make my mind pure in that same way.
The Ritual Procedure for the Kālacakra Pūjā: Free from possessiveness and free from ego, just as Vajradhara and the others are, so shall I dwell everywhere, unattached.

Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillfulness, aspiration, power, and knowledge— these ten perfections have been fully perfected by the heroes who are the enemies of Māra.
In that way, with my mind always fixed upon it, I shall fulfill it.
May my intention always be one of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings, and may I remain free from the worldly dharmas.

May I always be devoted to these— generosity, sweet speech, and constant engagement in beneficial conduct— and through love, may I exist for the sake of enlightenment, so that the human condition is not in vain.
Violence toward living beings, theft, lust, sexual misconduct,
false speech, harshness, slander, and divisive talk.
Covetousness, thoughts of malice, and even wrong views are far removed from me; I shall not even listen to such talk, much less have any intention of acting upon it.
"I abandon remorse, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, and doubt, as well as the afflictions of passion, hatred, great delusion, and pride. And so it shall be.
Free from the outflows of desire, existence, ignorance, and views;
devoid of emptiness, cause, superimposition, and the formation of conditioned things—I am weary of existence, O Lord of Beings, and I pray for this one thing alone:
may I possess intense devotion at the feet of the glorious Guru.
When, through the view of non-apprehension, shall I teach emptiness by means of conventional non-apprehension, out of reverence for the accumulation of merit?
However, the reading of the *mātṛkā* in the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha* is always as follows: "In all directions, as many as there are those afflicted by physical and mental suffering,
[may they attain] oceans of happiness and joy."

By my merits, may the god rain in due season, may there be an abundance of crops, and may the world become prosperous; may the king be righteous—or what need is there for more? I, the virtuous one, bestow both merit and demerit, as well as this very body, upon all.
May the fruit of all these be for the sake of my awakening.
Whatever suffering there is in the world, may it all ripen upon me;
and by all the virtues of the Bodhisattvas, may the world be happy.
Without experiencing the suffering of the miserable realms and without the practice of austerities,
may the world attain Buddhahood with a single divine body.

Then, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra for the sake of completing the offerings: *Oṃ vajrasattvasamayamanupālaya vajrasattvatvenopatiṣṭha dṛḍho me bhava sutoṣyo me bhava supoṣyo me bhava anurakto me bhava sarvasiddhiṃ me prayaccha sarvakarmasu ca me cittaṃ śreyaṃ kuru hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ bhagavan sarvatathāgatavajra mā me muñca vajrī bhava mahāsamayasattva āḥ*.
Then, having recited "What has been done for the sake of all sentient beings," and so forth, at the time of dismissal, one should contemplate as follows:
having honored the Teachers of the World with offerings of body, speech, and mind, one should reflect upon oneself as giving the cry of "Well done! (sādhukāra).
By this merit, may all sentient beings become perfectly awakened;
may the Sugatas remain in their own abodes until the coming day.

Whether it be that very [rite], or that, or that, or the ritual procedure for the worship of Kālacakra, until the final twilight— she should contemplate herself following her husband in the performance of the three-twilight worship.
Then, having received her husband's command, she returned home once again.
By whatever merit I have gained by thus performing the rite of worship for my husband, may the entire world become a vessel for the knowledge of the Omniscient One.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the worship of the Blessed Kālacakra.
The supplementary section on the Kālacakra maṇḍala:

Within the Vajrapañjara of the Kālacakra maṇḍala is the ten-spoked protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*). On its eastern, southern, western, and northern spokes are Atibala, Kumbhaka, Jambhaka, and Mānavaka—also known by the alternative names Vighnāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Yamāntaka, and Prajñāntaka.
On the spokes starting from the southeast are Nīladaṇḍa, Ṭakkirāja, Mahābala, and Acala.
At the upper extremity is Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, and at the lower extremity is Sumbharāja;
as it is stated in the Root [Tantra]: "Afterwards, one should visualize a host of wrathful deities pervading the wheel in the ten directions."
Thus [it is said].
And in the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated that the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) consisting of the wrathful deities and others should be emanated for the sake of protecting the mandala ground.
These wrathful deities, whose forms will be described below, are the *dharmodayās* within the center of the protection wheel.
As it is said in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Externally, the cause of origination is the infinite space-element; internally, it is wisdom (*prajñā*), the *dharmodayā*, which is triangular."
Indeed, the space-element itself is meditated upon as having the form of the *dharmodaya* within the mandala.

In the center of the *dharmodaya*, situated upon the wind, fire, water, and earth mandalas, Mount Sumeru, a universal lotus, and the moon and sun, stands the mandala of Rāhu in the form of a blue drop. Above this is the great peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), surrounded by the external vajra-fence and the elements of space, wind, fire, water, and earth; or else, there is the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) for the sole purpose of pacifying obstacles.

Immediately after destroying the obstacles, without further reflection and without meditating upon the *dharmodayā*, one should visualize within the protective cage (*rakṣāpañjara*) a great peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). This pavilion stands above the mandalas of the elements beginning with wind and ending with the mandala of Rāhu in the sphere of space, and is surrounded on the outside by garlands of light and so forth.

Within it is the mandala of speech, half the size of that; within that, the mandala of mind; within that, the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), half the size of that; within that, the green lotus of the Blessed One;
and at one-third of the lotus is the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Above that, upon the stacked mandalas of the Moon, Sun, Rāhu, and Kālāgni, the Lord Kālacakra dances in the *ālīḍha* posture between the face-down Ananga and the heart of Rudra; he is black, wears a crown of matted hair marked with a jewel, a half-moon, and a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), and is adorned with a vajra-jewel earring, a vajra necklace, a vajra breast-chain, a vajra belt, vajra anklets, a vajra head-band, and a vajra garland; he wears a garment of tiger skin and a human skin, possesses twelve eyes and four faces.

Then, the root face is black, fierce with terrifying fangs; the eastern face is red and passionate; the western face is yellow and established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*); and the northern face is white and peaceful.
The Lord has three necks, which are blue, red, and white, resting upon the right and left [shoulders].

The first right shoulder is blue, the second red, and the third white; likewise, the left [shoulders] are blue, red, and white. Thus, he has six shoulders and twelve arms; starting from the upper arms, there are twenty-four thousand [fingers]. Among them, two right arms are blue, two are red, and two are white, and likewise for the left.
Thus, there are four hands that are black, four that are red, and four that are white; those on the right and left are pleasing.
There are five fingers, each having three joints.
Among them, the thumb is yellow, the index finger is white, the middle finger is red, the ring finger is black, and the little finger is green.
From the palm, the first row of joints of all the fingers is black, the second is red, and the third is white.

And those [hands] are radiant with seals: in the right hands, the black ones hold a vajra, a sword, and a trident; the red ones hold fire, an arrow, and a vajra-hook; and the white ones hold a wheel, a spear, a staff, and an axe.

In the left hands, the black ones hold a vajra-bell, a shield, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) with an open mouth, and a skull-cup filled with blood; the red ones hold a bow, a noose, a jewel, and a lotus; and the white ones hold a mirror, a vajra, a chain, and the head of Brahmā.

From the thighs upward, Kāma is red in color; his right foot and sole are red, and he stands with his heart stepped upon by [Śiva’s] red left foot. He is red in color, has one face, four arms, and holds five flower-arrows, a bow, a noose, and a goad. From the thighs upward, Rudra is white; his left foot and sole are white, and he stands with his heart stepped upon by [Kāma’s] white right foot. He is brilliant white, has three eyes and one face, and holds a trident, a *ḍamaruka* drum, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff in his four arms. Beside Kāmadeva is Rati, and beside Maheśvara is Gaurī.
These two goddesses hold the feet of the Blessed One with dejected faces.

The Mother of the Universe (Viśvamātā), embraced by the Blessed One, stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, is golden-hued, and holds in her right hands a flaying knife (*kartṛkā*), a goad (*aṅkuśa*), a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), and a rosary (*akṣasūtra*); and in her left hands, a spear (*śakti*), a noose (*pāśa*), a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), and a jewel (*ratna*).

On the eastern petal is Kṛṣṇā Dīptā, who is black in color and holds in her right hands an incense burner (*dhūpakaṭacchū*), a sandalwood vessel, a saffron vessel, and a camphor vessel containing musk; and in her left hands, a bell (*ghaṇṭā*), a lotus, a flower from the celestial tree (*surataru*), and a garland of various flowers.

In the south is Raktadīptā, who is red in color; she holds a lamp, a necklace, a crown, and a bracelet with her right hands, and a garment, a girdle, a jeweled earring, and an anklet with her left hands. In the west is Pīṭhadīptā, who is yellow in color; she holds a conch, a flute, a jewel, and a hand-drum (ḍamaru) with her right hands, and a lute, a large drum (ḍhakkā), a cymbal (kaṃsikā), and a trumpet (kāhalā) with her left hands.

In the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, in the northern direction is Śvetadīptā, who is white in color. With her right hands she holds a vessel of milk, a vessel of water, a divine medicine, and a vessel of wine; with her left hands she holds a vessel of nectar (*amṛta*), a vessel of the elixir of accomplishment (*siddharasa*), a fruit of immortality, and a vessel of cooked rice. In the directions beginning with the southeast (Agni), there are the goddesses Dhūmā, Marīcī, Pratipā, and Khadyotā, who are respectively black, red, yellow, and white in color. Each has eight arms holding eight fly-whisks (*cāmara*) of their own respective colors.
Behind them, on the outside, are the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), the Dharma-gong, the wish-granting tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), and the Dharma-conch, which are black, red, yellow, and white.
The eight [deities] beginning with Kṛṣṇadīptā stand on even ground.
All the goddesses, beginning with Viśvamātā, possess the five mudrās, have eight arms, twelve eyes, and four faces.
Among them, the faces of Viśvamātā, in the order of east, south, west, and north, are yellow, white, blue, and red.
The same applies to the yellow goddesses.
For the black [goddesses], however, the colors are black, red, yellow, and white; for the red [goddesses], red, yellow, white, and blue; and for the white [goddesses], white, black, red, and yellow.
The deities in the second and third enclosures have three eyes, three faces, and six arms.

There, in the eastern direction, is Amoghasiddhi, who is black with faces that are black, red, and white. With his right hands he holds a sword, a single-edged knife, and a trident; with his left hands he holds a shield, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*. He is embraced by Locanā. In the southern direction is Ratnasambhava, who is red with faces that are red, white, and black. With his right hands he holds a fire-arrow, a vajra-hook, and a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*); with his left hands he holds a bow and a nine-faceted jewel. He is embraced by Māmakī.

In the west is Vairocana, yellow in color, with faces that are yellow, white, and black. He holds a wheel, a staff, and a hand-gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in his right hands, and a sword, a vajra, a chain, and a vajra-bell in his left hands; he is embraced by Tārā. In the north is Amitābha, white in color, with faces that are white, black, and red. He holds a mallet, a spear, and a trident in his right hands, and a lotus, a mirror, and a rosary in his left hands; he is embraced by Pāṇḍarā.

These four [deities] stand upon white lotuses and sun discs, wear crowns of matted hair, and have faces colored respectively red in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast, situated upon moon discs on red lotuses. They are Tārā, Pāṇḍarā, Locanā, and Māmakī, who correspond in color to Amoghasiddhi, Ratneśa, Śāśvata, and Amitābha, and are in union with Vairocana, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Ratnasambhava. For Tārā, there may be a blue lotus in place of the khaṭvāṅga. In the eight armpits are eight nectar-filled jars.

In the third enclosure, on the frieze to the left of the eastern gate, is Samantabhadra, blue in color. He holds a vajra, a flaying knife, and an axe in his right hands, and a bell, a skull-cup, and the head of Brahmā in his left hands; alternatively, there may be an utpala lotus in place of the head of Brahmā.
He is in union with Dharmavajrā.
To the right is Khagarbha, who, like Amoghasiddhi, is embraced by Gandhavajrā.

At the southern gate is Vajrapāṇi, green in color, holding a vajra, a flaying knife, and an axe in his right hands, and a bell, a skull-cup, and the head of Brahmā in his left hands; he is embraced by Śabdavajrā.
Kṣitigarbha is like Ratnasambhava in appearance and is embraced by Rūpavajrā.
At the western gate is Dharmadhātuvajra, who is like Vajrapāṇi and is embraced by Samantabhadra.
Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin is like Vairocana and is embraced by Sparśavajrā. At the northern gate, Śabdavajrā is embraced by Vajrapāṇi, who is like Samantabhadra-vajra.
Lokeśvara resembles Amitābha and is embraced by Rasavajrā.
In the intermediate directions, in the southeast is Sparśavajrā, who is in union with Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin like Tārā;
in the southwest is Rasavajrā, embraced by Lokeśvara like Pāṇḍarā;
in the northwest is Gandhavajrā, embraced by Khagarbha like Locanā.
In the northeast is Rūpavajrā, who, like Māmakī, is embraced by Kṣitigarbha.
Here, the Tathāgatas such as Amoghasiddhi and the Bodhisattvas are seated upon vajra-thrones,
while the goddesses beginning with Tārā are seated upon lotus-thrones.
At the eastern gate is Atibalakrodha, like Amoghasiddhi, embraced by Stambhikī;
she, however, is like Locanā!
At the southern [gate] is Jambhaka, like Ratnasambhava, absorbed in union with Māmakī.
She, however, is equal to Māmakī.
In the western pillar is Vairocana, embraced by Atibalā; she, moreover, is like Tārā.
In the north is Mānaka, like Amitāyus, embraced by Jambhakī;
she, however, is like Pāṇḍarā. But these wrathful deities (krodhas) stand in the ālīḍha posture, while the wrathful goddesses (krodhadevis) stand in the pratyālīḍha posture.
In this context, the seats for male deities are white lotuses situated upon sun discs;
for female deities, they are red lotuses with moon discs.
Alternatively, [the male deities] are black, white, or green, seated on moons, while the female deities are red or yellow.
The Samantabhadras and the Śabdavajras are situated upon solar mandalas.

Regarding the arrangement in rows, it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "In this context, whichever deity is mentioned in a particular place, she is positioned facing the central deity of the maṇḍala due to her preeminence, but she does not exist here [in this case] seated on his lap.

Where the goddess is depicted holding a bell, a Dharma-conch, and so forth, and the mind-maṇḍala consisting of twenty-five aspects is meditated upon, there the Blessed One is also seated, as in the *Śrī-samāja*.
In the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, on the altar: to the east, to the left of the base of the left arch-pillar, is Gandhā, black in color, holding a scent-conch in her hand;
to the right of the right [pillar], is Mālā, blue in color, holding a garland of flowers;
and to the south, is Dhūpā, red in color, holding an incense burner in her hand.
Dīpā is red and holds a lamp-stand;
in the west is Lāsyā, yellow, wearing a yellow crown;
Hāsyā is yellow and wears a yellow necklace.

In the north is Amitā, also known as Amṛtanaivedyā, white in color and holding a fruit in her hand; she is also known as Halā, Akṣatā, and Amṛtaphalā, and holds a vessel filled with nectar in her hand. On all the altars, there are innumerable various goddesses who uphold the worship and offerings (pūjā-naivedya-devīs). At the position of the worship-goddess on the eastern archway is Nṛtyā, blue in color, who has taken up a cloth for the performance of a dance.
In the south is Kāmā, red in color and holding a lotus in her hand; in the west is Vādyā, yellow, playing a *paṭaha* drum;
in the north is Gītā, white, holding a vajra.
This placement (*nyāsa*) of Amṛtā and the others follows the sequence explained in the commentary on the *Abhiṣeka-paṭala*. As it was stated in the commentary on the *Sādhana-paṭala*:

"In the north are Vādī, Nṛtyā, Ākāśagītā, and Kāmā; below are Naivedyā, Amṛtā, and Phalā. In that case as well, the placement (*nyāsa*) mentioned in the *Sekapaṭala* should be understood by means of a textual arrangement consistent with that [statement], for otherwise there would be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
These twelve goddesses are seated upon lotus postures.
In the circle of speech (*vāṅmaṇḍala*), the lotuses in the cardinal directions are red;
in the corners, which are devoid of the moon and sun, the goddesses are stationed on odd-numbered petals.

There, upon the pericarp of the eastern lotus situated above the *preta*, is Cāmuṇḍā, black in color, with three eyes and one face; she holds a flaying knife and a trident in her two right hands, and a skull-cup and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff in her two left hands, and is embraced by Indra.
On the eight petals starting from the east are Bhīmā, Ugrā, Kāladaṃṣṭrā, Jvalanmukhā, Vāyuvegā, Pracaṇḍā, Raudrākṣī, and Sthūlanāsā.

Upon the pericarp of the fire-lotus situated above Garuḍa is Vaiṣṇavī, who is black; she holds a discus and a mace in her two right hands and a lotus and a conch in her two left hands, and she is embraced by Brahmā. On the petals are Śrī, Māyā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Vijayā, Śrījayantī, and Śrīcakrī. The maṇḍala of the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra) is also there. Upon a buffalo, on the pericarp of the southern lotus, is Vārāhī, who is red and has the face of a boar.
In her two right hands she holds a staff and a sword; in her two left hands she holds a chain and a plough; she is embraced by Rudra.
On the petals are Kaṅkālī, Kālarātri, Prakupitavadanā, Kālajihvā, Karālī, Ghorā, and Virūpā;

on the pericarp of the lotus in the southwest, atop a peacock, is the red six-faced Kaumārī, holding a spear and a goad in her right hands and a jewel and a noose in her left hands, merged with Gaṇeśa;
on the petals are Padmā, Anaṅgā, Kumārī, Mṛgapatigamanā, Sunetrā, Līnā, and Subhadrā.

Upon Airāvata, on the pericarp of the western lotus, is Aindrī, yellow in color; she holds a vajra and an arrow in her two right hands and a bell and a bow in her two left hands, and is embraced by Nairṛti.
On the petals are Vajrābhā, Vajragātrā, Kanakāvatī, Ūrvaśī, Citralekhā, Rambhā, Ahalyā, and Sutārā.

Upon a swan, on the pericarp of the northwestern lotus, is Brahmāṇī, with a yellow face; she holds a lotus and a *brahmadaṇḍa* in her two right hands, and a water-pot and a vessel in her two left hands, and is united with Viṣṇu.

On the petals are Śāvitri, Padmanetrī, Jaladavatī, Buddhi, Vāgīśvarī, Gāyatrī, Vidyut, and Smṛti. On the northern petal, atop a bull, is Raudrī, who is white; she holds a trident and a *ḍamaru* in her right hands, and a *khaṭvāṅga* and an arrow in her left hands, and is embraced by Yama. On the petals are Gaurī, Gaṅgā, Nityā, Tvaritā, Totalā, Lakṣaṇā, Piṅgalā, and Kṛṣṇā. In the pericarp of the lotus is [the goddess] Śubhrā.

Upon a lion, in the pericarp of the lotus in the northeast, is Lakṣmī, white in color, holding a lotus and a rosary in her two right hands and a lotus and a jewel in her two left hands, embraced by Kārttikeya. On the petals are Śrī (white), Candralekhā (moon-crested, with a face like the moon), Haṃsavarṇā, Dhṛti, Padmeśā, and Vimalaśaśadharā. These seventy-two goddesses, beginning with Carcikā, have four arms, three eyes, and are white in color.

Here, the petal goddesses (*daladevī*), standing upon *lalita* (graceful) postures and possessing colors and other attributes identical to their respective principal consorts (*nāyikā*), gaze toward their own principal consorts;

these eight principal consorts stand upon *viśākha* (crossed) postures. The Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśa*) stands upon a *viśākha* posture embraced by those eight, while the secondary consorts (*anunāyikā*) face toward them.
In the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, within the body-mandala (*kāyamaṇḍala*), there are twelve lotuses on the bands (*paṭṭikā*) that are devoid of the moon and sun.

In that [mandala], the lotuses of the cardinal directions are red and those situated in the corners are white; the petals of each individual lotus are as follows: four in the first circle, eight in the second, and sixteen in the third.

Within these, starting from the petal in the east of the outermost circle and proceeding clockwise, there is the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the goddesses of the lunar days (tithis), one for each day.
In the pericarp (*karṇikā*), however, the full moon (*pūrṇimā*) and the new moon (*āmāvāsyā*) reside as the central lords;
therein, the full moon is wisdom (*prajñā*) and the new moon is method (*upāya*). All the deities, beginning with Nairṛti, have four arms.

There, in the pericarp upon a lotus situated on the right side of the eastern gate, atop a red corpse, is Nairṛti, who is black in color. He holds a sword and a flaying knife in his two right hands, and a shield and a skull-cup in his two left hands. His face has a blazing fire, and he is embraced by a Rākṣasī.

On the lunar days of Caitra, he stands upon a deer over a lotus situated on a *puṣkara*; he is dark blue in color, embraced by Pracaṇḍā, with a *kalpavṛkṣa* tree and a *pārijāta* flower in his right hands, and an indranīla gem and a blue lotus in his left hands.
These are his lunar days of Vaiśākha.

On the left of the southern gate, upon a buffalo, on the pericarp of a lotus, is Yama, red in color, embraced by Kālī; in his two right hands he holds a staff and a sword, and in his two left hands a chain and a noose. His lunar days are those of Phālguna.
On the right, on a ram, on the pericarp of a lotus, is Agni, red in color, embraced by Varuṇā; in his two right hands he holds a spear and a staff, and in his two left hands a lotus and a water-pot.

On a peacock atop a lotus in the southwest (Nairṛtya), upon its pericarp, is the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), red in color, holding a spear and a water-pot in his two right hands and a jewel and a mirror in his two left hands, united with Lakṣmī; these are his lunar days of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Now, his lunar days of the month of Āṣāḍha:

To the left of the western gate, upon an elephant on the pericarp of a lotus, is Kubera, yellow in color, embraced by Kauberī; he holds a jewel and a mace in his two right hands, and a mongoose and a lotus in his two left hands.
His lunar days are those of the month of Pauṣa.

To the right, upon an elephant on the tip of a lotus, is Śakra, yellow in color, embraced by Vāsavī; he holds a vajra and a fire-arrow in his two right hands, and a bell and a bow in his two left hands.

For the lunar days of Aśvinī, in the northwest upon a swan, on the pericarp of a lotus, is yellow Brahmā embraced by Vidyut; in his two right hands he holds a needle and a rosary, and in his two left hands a lotus and a water-pot.
For the lunar days of Kārttika, [he is] as follows.

To the left of the northern gate, upon a bull on the pericarp of a lotus, is Rudra, white in color and embraced by Gaurī; in his two right hands he holds a trident and an arrow, and in his two left hands a khaṭvāṅga entwined with a snake and a bow. His lunar days are those of Mārgaśīrṣa, and his maṇḍala is that of Kālacakra. To the right, upon a crocodile on the pericarp of a lotus, is the Ocean, white in color and embraced by Vārāhī; in his two right hands he holds a noose and a jewel, and in his two left hands a nāga-noose and a moonstone gem. His lunar days are those of Śrāvaṇa.

In the northeast, upon a mouse on the pericarp of a lotus, is Gaṇeśa, white in color; he holds an axe and a thunderbolt in his two right hands and a noose and a goad in his two left hands, and is united with Kaumārī.
His lunar days are Bhadra and Pūrṇimā.

To the left of the eastern door, upon Garuḍa on the pericarp of a lotus, is Viṣṇu, black in color, united with Śrī; he holds a discus and a mace in his two right hands and a lotus and a conch in his two left hands.

Here, the lunar days of the month of Māgha are the goddesses beginning with Caitrī, seated upon vajra-thrones and possessing graceful steps; they behold all their respective lords, starting from Nairṛta, who are established with their specific colors, weapons, and postures.
And those [goddesses], embraced by them, behold the Lord of the Maṇḍala.
At the eastern gate, Nīladaṇḍa is in a black chariot drawn by seven black boars, like Amoghasiddhi;
embraced by him, Mārīcī is yellow, holding a discus and a staff in her two right hands and a conch and a jewel in her two left hands.
To the south, in a red chariot drawn by seven red horses, is Ṭakkirāja, like Ratneśa.

Cundā, embraced by him, is white; she holds a mallet and a spear in her two right hands and the stalks of two lotuses in her two left hands. On a yellow chariot drawn by seven yellow elephants in the west is Mahābala, who is like Vairocana. Embraced by him, Vajraśṛṅkhalā is black; she holds a jewel and a vajra in her two right hands and a flask and a snake in her two left hands.

In the north, on a white chariot drawn by seven white lions, is Acala, who is Amitābha; he embraces Bhṛkuṭī, who is red. With his two right hands he holds an arrow and a goad, and with his two left hands a bow and a noose. Above the wheel, in the sky, is Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, borne by a five-colored Garuḍa with three eyes, riding a green chariot like Vajrapāṇi.

His consort, Bhadravati, is deep blue in color; she holds a flaying knife and a vajra in her two right hands, and a skull-cup and a bell in her two left. Below the Lord of the Mandala (Cakreśa), in the subterranean realm (pātāla), Sumbharāja stands upon a black chariot drawn by eight-legged black tigers. In the *Samantacakratantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, it is stated that his consort Raudrākṣī is green; she carries an axe and a trident in her two right hands, and a snake-noose and a khaṭvāṅga staff in her two left.
Therein, the wrathful deities beginning with Nīladaṇḍa stand in the ālīḍha posture upon white lotuses and sun disks atop the chariots.

The male leaders, remaining in their respective places, gaze upon the Lord of the Mandala; however, Mārīcī and the others, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, gaze upon the wrathful deities because they have gone to the locations of others.
The female consorts, by going to the locations of others, gaze upon the wrathful deities.
In this context, the chariots possess colors such as black and others according to their lineage;
this is established by the statement "the chariot is in the middle of the door," and accordingly, the same applies to the boars and other [deities].
In the middle of the gateway pillars, at the location of the altar, there are hooded serpents above and below.
There, on the left and right of the eastern gate, within the two wind-mandalas, are the black Padma and Karkoṭaka, embraced respectively by Śvānāsyā and Kākāsyā.
On the two fire-mandalas of the southern gate are the red Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla, joined with Śūkarāsyā and Gṛdhrāsyā.

Takṣaka and Mahāpadma, yellow in color, embrace [the two goddesses] at the western door upon the earth mandalas; Jambukāsyā and Garuḍāsyā are at the northern door upon the water mandalas; Ananta and Kulika, white in color, are at the upper sky upon the space mandala; and Jaya, green in color, is embraced by Nīlā.
Below, in the empty maṇḍala of Pātāla, is Vijaya, blue in color, in union with Vajrākṣī;
all the nāgas are seated upon vajra-thrones, four-armed, holding a jar of nectar and a vajra in their two right hands, and a lotus and a jewel in their two left hands;
in the northeast of the earth-girdle is the risen full-moon maṇḍala.

As the sun sets in the southwest, in the midst of the circles of fire and wind, there are eight-spoked wheels in the great cremation grounds; those in the cardinal directions are red, and those in the intermediate directions are white.
Here, on the eastern wheel, Śvānāsyā is black; on the southern, Śūkarāsyā is red; on the western, Jambukāsyā is yellow; and on the northern, Vyāghrāsyā is white.
In the directions beginning with the southeast (Āgneyī), there are Kākāsyā, Gṛdhrāsyā, Garuḍāsyā, and Ulūkāsyā, who are black, red, yellow, and white respectively.
In the upper direction of space, there is Anilā, who is blue in color; her chariot is like that of Anilā.
In the Kālacakra maṇḍala, at the bottom on the Pātāla chariot is Vajrākṣī, who is green;
her chariot is like that of Raudrākṣī.

These [deities], beginning with Śvānāsyā, stand upon the positions of the maṇḍala, embraced by the previously mentioned Padmā and others. They hold a curved knife and a skull-cup in their right and left hands respectively, possess three eyes, are naked, wear the five mudrās, and have garlands of severed heads hanging from their necks.
And on the floors of the first eight [terraces], in successive order, there are, respectively, a rhinoceros, a bear, a lion, a yak, a bheruṇḍa, a krauñca crane, a blue-eyed bird, and a vāgavali.

In these very cremation grounds, within the wind-circle (*vāyu-valaya*), the moon and sun are situated in the eastern and southeastern directions within the wind-mandala; Mercury and Mars are in the southern and southwestern directions within the fire-mandala; Ketu and Saturn are in the western and northwestern directions within the earth-mandala; Venus and Jupiter are in the northern and northeastern directions within the water-mandala; Rāhu is in the upper void-mandala, and Kālāgni is in the lower void-mandala. Furthermore, within this wind-circle are Dhruva, Agastya, the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśis*), the sixteen digits (*kalās*), the ten guardians of the directions (*dig-lokapālas*), the field-protectors (*kṣetrapālas*)—namely Nandin, Mahākāla, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and Bhṛṅgin—the female messengers (*dūtīs*), Hārītī, all the *siddhis*, and so forth, including three and a half million distinct types of spirits (*bhūta-viśeṣas*), possessing various colors, symbols, and forms.

Here, the deities beginning with Candra are seated upon vajra-thrones, while the goddesses are in the *lalita* posture. Within the altars of the maṇḍala of Speech (*vāṅmaṇḍala*), there are the goddesses of Will (*icchādevī*).

Among them, on the eastern altar, in the southern direction of the door, is Vidveṣecchā (the Will for Enmity), who is like Tārā; Aṃśukēcchā (the Will for Clothing), who is like Sparśavajrā; Kāyakaṇḍūyanēcchā (the Will for Scratching the Body), who is like Cāmuṇḍā; Vadanakaphōtsarjanēcchā (the Will for Discharging Phlegm from the Mouth), who is like Vaiṣṇavī; and Uccāṭanēcchā (the Will for Expulsion), who is like Atibalā.

To the left of the door: the desire for tormenting is like Atinīlā; the desire for touch is like Vajraśṛṅkhalā; the desire to toss all limbs about is like Vārāhī; the desire for boiled rice is like Śvānāsyā; the desire for discarded food is like Kākāsyā. To the right of the door: the desire for paralyzing is like Pāṇḍarā; the desire for eating is like Rasavajrā; the desire for bodily filth is like Vārāhī; the desire for dancing is like Kaumārī; the desire for withering is like Jambhanī. On the left: the desire for attracting is like Bhṛkuṭī; the desire for running is like Raudrākṣī; the desire to suppress urine and feces is like Śūkarāsyā; the desire for battle is like Gṛdhrāsyā.

To the left of the western door: Locanā, who desires to paralyze; Gandhavajrā, who desires fragrance; Aindrī, who desires a bed; Brahmāṇī, who desires to flood with drink; Stambhanī, who desires to bind;
on the left [side], Dharmadhātuvajrā, who desires sexual union; Mārīcī, who desires to pierce; Jambukāsyā, who desires to strike with a vajra; and Garuḍāsyā, who desires to bind snakes.

In the *Kālacakra-tantra-laghugrantha-saṃgraha*, on the right side of the northern gate, one should visualize these thirty-six goddesses: Puṣṭīcchā like Māmakī; Bhūṣaṇecchā with Rūpavajrā; Āsaneccchā like Raudrī; Rājyecchā like Lakṣmī; Mṛduvacanecchā like Māmakī; on the left, Vādyecchā like Śabdavajrā; Bandhanecchā like Cundā; Bahukalahecchā like Vyāghrāsyā; and Dārakakrīḍanecchā like Ulūkāsyā. These are the thirty-six goddesses to be visualized.

As for what was stated— that the desire for slaying is subsumed within the desire generated by Vajradhātvīśvarī, and the desire for generation is subsumed within that generated by Viśvamātṛ— these two desires are included within the other desires as appropriate,
rather than being treated separately; with this very intention, whatever other desires there may be, they are all to be subsumed within these thirty-six desires as appropriate.
And because the single desire is intended as an inclusive indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), it is said that "there are thirty-seven desires.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Whatever other activity for the sake of sentient beings there may be that is [driven by] desire, all of that is performed by the Yoginīs through the power of the mantra-element.
Therefore, it is taught that only thirty-six seed-syllables (*bīja*) are to be placed within the colored powder mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*).

However, in that context, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seed-syllable *śaṃ* for the desire to kill is said to be on the left of the eastern gate; the seed-syllable *kaṃ* for the desire to deceive is on the left of the southern gate; and the seed-syllable *laṃ* for the desire to bind with snakes is on the left of the northern gate.

But such is not the case in the visualization of the Goddesses of Desire (*icchādevī*), as stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "In the mandala of the thirty-seven desires, [they are placed] in their respective directions according to the divisions of their own respective families."
And all of this must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, there would be mutual contradiction among the many statements such as "the thirty-six desires," and so forth.

The counter-desires (*pratīcchā*), which are the nature of the cessation of these desires, are thirty-six. On the altars of the body-maṇḍalas, as before, according to their respective families, in their own directions, all the deities other than the Tathāgatas—the Lords of the Wheels (*cakreśa*) and so on—are adorned with crowns of various jewels.
In this context, when the Blessed One Kālacakra is established as having the nature of Vajrasattva, he is sealed by Akṣobhya of green color;
likewise, when Viśvamātā has the nature of Akṣobhya, she is [sealed] by Vajrasattva in the form of blue Akṣobhya.
Thus, Viśvamātā has the nature of Dharmadhātvīśvarī.
In this way, there occurs the mutual sealing of gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

As it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "The Mother of the Universe, who is not born from the pledge of the supreme Victor, is the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*) and the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).
Here, gnosis is the gnosis of imperishable great bliss, which is of a single flavor with emptiness and compassion.
When, however, Kālacakra is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), then Viśvamātā is by nature Ākāśadhātu and Vajradhātvīśvarī; this is the meaning.

Therefore it is said: "The Kālacakra mandala is indicated by Vajradhātvīśvarī as Viśvamātā. Thus, consciousness together with Vajradhātvīśvarī [is located] in the lotus of the womb, that is, in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
Amoghasiddhi, Ratneśa, Vairocana, and Amitābha are sealed by the green Akṣobhya.

Alternatively, Ratnasambhava is sealed by Amoghasiddhi, Vairocana by Amitābha, and Akṣobhya by the green Samantabhadra; Śabdavajrā, Sumbharāja, Atinīlā, Anilā, Rudra, Jambhala, and Vijayanāga are sealed by Vajrasattva in the form of blue Akṣobhya; while Vajrapāṇi, Dharmadhātuvajrā, Uṣṇīṣacakrī, Raudrākṣī, Viṣṇu, Yama, and Jayanāga are sealed by green Akṣobhya.
Furthermore, the other deities are black by Amoghasiddhi, red by Ratnasambhava, yellow by Vairocana, and white by Amitābha;
these Tathāgatas possess the six mudrās, have uṣṇīṣas, wear monastic robes, and display the earth-touching and other mudrās.
The heart-seed syllable of the Blessed One, the Lord of the Wheel, is *hūṃ*;
however, the other mantras are not stated here for fear of prolixity,
and thus the immeasurable perfections of his forms remain unspoken.
The cloud draws up the inexhaustible water from the ocean;

the Lord of Beings, Abhaya, who acts for the sake of others, becomes like a limitless form through the surging streams of nectar of merit that overflow from the nectar-flow of the form of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Indra), as if through mutually intermingling forms.
Thus concludes the Kālacakra maṇḍala.
This *Niṣpannayogāvalī* is completed.
